milky-way.name: Milky Way
milky-way.introduction: is our home galaxy, a barred spiral about 87,000 light-years across with 100–400 billion stars. The Sun lies about 27,000 light-years from its center, which hides behind thick dust in Sagittarius. Seen from inside, the disk wraps around the sky as a hazy band of light.

image.alt: The band of the Milky Way across the sky, with dark dust lanes over the bright Galactic Center.
image.caption: ESO/S. Brunier · visible-light all-sky mosaic · released 2009
image.credit: ESO/S. Brunier. Visible-light all-sky mosaic, released 2009. Cropped to the central 120° × 60° around the Galactic Center, resized to 600 × 300 and converted to AVIF; colors unchanged.

sections.title: One galaxy among many
sections.text: Galileo Galilei first resolved the hazy band into individual stars with his telescope in 1610. Until the early 1920s, most astronomers thought the Milky Way held every star in the universe. After the 1920 Great Debate between Harlow Shapley and Heber Curtis, observations by Edwin Hubble in 1923 showed that it is just one of many galaxies.

sections.title: A black hole at the heart
sections.text: At the center sits the radio source Sagittarius A*, a supermassive black hole of about 4.1 million solar masses. The Event Horizon Telescope imaged its shadow in radio waves, published in 2022. Around it, the innermost 10,000 light-years hold a bulge of mostly old stars, from which the galaxy’s bar extends.

sections.title: Measured by a single star
sections.text: The star S2 circles Sagittarius A* every 16 years on a long, narrow orbit. Astronomers followed it for 27 years, and from 2017 the GRAVITY instrument measured its offset from the black hole to as little as 20 millionths of an arcsecond. Its orbit puts the center 8,178 parsecs away, about 26,700 light-years, to 0.3%.

source.title: GRAVITY Collaboration (2019): A geometric distance measurement to the Galactic center black hole with 0.3% uncertainty

sections.title: One lap in 212 million years
sections.text: Stars away from the bulge and the outer rim orbit the center at 200–220 km/s, almost regardless of their distance from it. The Sun takes about 212 million years for one lap.

large-magellanic-cloud.name: Large Magellanic Cloud
large-magellanic-cloud.introduction: is the largest satellite galaxy of the Milky Way, about 162,000 light-years away across Dorado and Mensa. To the naked eye it is a faint cloud about 10° long, 20 times the Moon’s diameter. It holds the Tarantula Nebula, the most active star-forming region in the Local Group.

image.alt: The Large Magellanic Cloud: a bright bluish bar of stars with pink star-forming nebulae above it.
image.caption: CTIO/NOIRLab/NSF/AURA/SMASH/D. Nidever (Montana State University) · SMASH survey · released 2020
image.credit: CTIO/NOIRLab/NSF/AURA/SMASH/D. Nidever (Montana State University). Image processing: Travis Rector (University of Alaska Anchorage), Mahdi Zamani and Davide de Martin. Released 2020. Cropped to the galaxy, resized to 600 × 349 and converted to AVIF; colors unchanged.

source.title: NOIRLab: Deepest, widest view of the Large Magellanic Cloud from SMASH

sections.title: Bound for the Milky Way
sections.text: The bar at its center suggests that the cloud was once a barred dwarf spiral, until the pull of the Small Magellanic Cloud and the Milky Way disrupted its arms. Its story is not over: the Large Magellanic Cloud is predicted to merge with the Milky Way in about 2.4 billion years.

sections.title: Heavy enough to bend a stream
sections.text: The Orphan stream is a long trail of stars orbiting the Milky Way. Its stars move at an angle to the trail, a sign of a large gravitational kick. Modeling that kick weighs the Large Magellanic Cloud at about 140 billion solar masses, dark matter included, enough to disturb other structures orbiting the Milky Way.

source.title: Erkal et al. (2019): The total mass of the Large Magellanic Cloud from its perturbation on the Orphan stream

sections.title: The cosmic yardstick’s anchor
sections.text: Cepheid variable stars measure distances to other galaxies, but they must first be calibrated in a galaxy whose distance is known. The Large Magellanic Cloud has long been that anchor. In 2019, eclipsing binaries of cool late-type stars measured its distance to 1%, a key step toward a 1% value of the Hubble constant.

source.title: Pietrzyński et al. (2019): A distance to the Large Magellanic Cloud that is precise to one per cent

sections.title: Two bright Canopi
sections.text: A claimed mention by the Persian astronomer al-Sufi around 964 seems to refer to other stars. The first confirmed record is a letter by Amerigo Vespucci from 1502, which mentions “three Canopi, two bright and one obscure”: the two Magellanic Clouds and the dark Coalsack. Ferdinand Magellan saw the cloud on his 1519 voyage, and it now bears his name.

sections.title: A celestial treasure house
sections.text: Rich in gas and dust, the cloud is still forming stars at a brisk pace. Surveys have found about 60 globular clusters, 400 planetary nebulae and 700 open clusters, along with hundreds of thousands of giant and supergiant stars. Supernova 1987A, the nearest supernova in recent years, exploded here.

small-magellanic-cloud.name: Small Magellanic Cloud
small-magellanic-cloud.introduction: is a dwarf galaxy orbiting the Milky Way, about 204,000 light-years away across Tucana and part of Hydrus. It is one of the most distant objects visible to the naked eye, a faint hazy patch about 4.2° across, eight times the Moon’s width. Its Cepheid stars gave astronomers their first ruler for the universe.

image.alt: The Small Magellanic Cloud: a bluish, irregular cloud of stars with pink star-forming nebulae.
image.caption: CTIO/NOIRLab/NSF/AURA/SMASH/D. Nidever (Montana State University) · SMASH survey · released 2020
image.credit: CTIO/NOIRLab/NSF/AURA/SMASH/D. Nidever (Montana State University). Image processing: Travis Rector (University of Alaska Anchorage), Mahdi Zamani and Davide de Martin. Released 2020. Resized to 600 × 500 and converted to AVIF; colors unchanged.

source.title: NOIRLab: Deepest, widest view of the Small Magellanic Cloud from SMASH

sections.title: The ruler for the universe
sections.text: Henrietta Swan Leavitt at Harvard studied photographic plates of the cloud taken in Arequipa, Peru. In 1908 she published that the variable stars now called Cepheids brighten and fade on periods that follow their brightness. Because all of the cloud’s stars lie at about the same distance, this meant a link between period and true luminosity: Cepheids became standard candles.

sections.title: Deeper than it is wide
sections.text: Fifteen eclipsing binaries measured the cloud’s distance to better than 2%. They also revealed its shape: the binaries form an elongated structure, steeply tilted to the sky. The nearest and the farthest system differ by 10 kiloparsecs, about 33,000 light-years, along the line of sight.

source.title: Graczyk et al. (2020): A distance determination to the Small Magellanic Cloud with an accuracy of better than two percent

sections.title: Two clouds in one?
sections.text: One study proposed that a past encounter with the Large Magellanic Cloud split the small cloud, and named the smaller piece the Mini Magellanic Cloud. In 2023, another found two separate structures with distinct chemical compositions in their stars and gas, about 5 kiloparsecs apart.

sections.title: A bridge to its big sister
sections.text: A bridge of gas, where new stars are forming, links the Small Magellanic Cloud to the Large one, evidence of their tidal pull on each other. The two share an envelope of hydrogen gas, a sign that they have been bound together for a long time. The small cloud’s central bar hints that it, too, was once a barred spiral.

andromeda-galaxy.name: Andromeda Galaxy
andromeda-galaxy.introduction: is the nearest large spiral galaxy and the largest member of the Local Group, about 2.5 million light-years away in Andromeda. At magnitude 3.4 it is visible to the naked eye on moonless nights, even under moderate light pollution. Also known as Messier 31 or NGC 224, it is moving toward the Milky Way.

image.alt: The Andromeda Galaxy seen at a steep angle, with a bright yellowish core, dark dust lanes and its two small companion galaxies.
image.caption: Adam Evans · visible light with hydrogen-alpha · 2010
image.credit: Adam Evans. Visible light with a hydrogen-alpha layer, 2010. Resized to 600 × 394 and converted to AVIF; colors unchanged.

sections.title: The little cloud
sections.text: Around 964, the Persian astronomer al-Sufi described a “small cloud” in his Book of Fixed Stars. It is the first known reference to a galaxy other than the Milky Way, and star charts of the period labeled it the Little Cloud.

sections.title: Proof of other galaxies
sections.text: Whether the “Great Andromeda Nebula” lay inside the Milky Way was long disputed. In 1922, Ernst Öpik estimated from the speeds of its stars that it lay far outside. Edwin Hubble settled the debate in 1925: on photographs taken with the 100-inch Hooker telescope he found Cepheid variables, whose distance showed an entirely separate galaxy.

sections.title: Collision course?
sections.text: Andromeda approaches the Milky Way at about 110 km/s, one of only about 100 galaxies seen with a blueshift. Once its sideways motion was measured, a direct collision was predicted in about 4 billion years. Later calculations with Gaia data and the pull of other Local Group galaxies gave a much lower chance: about 50% in the next 10 billion years.

sections.title: A ring of fire
sections.text: Its gas and dust lie in several overlapping rings. The most prominent, 32,000 light-years from the core, is nicknamed the ring of fire. Made mainly of cold dust, it hides from visible light, yet most of the galaxy’s star formation happens there. Infrared images from Spitzer show two segmented spiral arms emerging from a central bar.

sections.title: Measured to 1.5%
sections.text: Hubble Space Telescope observations of 55 Cepheids, in the same three filters used to calibrate them in the Large Magellanic Cloud, give a distance of 761,000 parsecs, about 2.48 million light-years, uncertain by just 1.5%.

source.title: Li et al. (2021): A Sub-2% Distance to M31 from Photometrically Homogeneous Near-infrared Cepheid Period–Luminosity Relations

triangulum-galaxy.name: Triangulum Galaxy
triangulum-galaxy.introduction: is a spiral galaxy about 2.7 million light-years away in Triangulum, the third-largest member of the Local Group after the Andromeda Galaxy and the Milky Way. Under a truly dark sky, some people can just see it without optical aid, which makes it the most distant permanent object visible to the naked eye. It is also known as Messier 33 or NGC 598.

image.alt: The Triangulum Galaxy seen nearly face-on, with loose spiral arms dotted by pink star-forming regions.
image.caption: T. A. Rector (NRAO/AUI/NSF and NOIRLab/NSF/AURA) and M. Hanna (NOIRLab/NSF/AURA) · Kitt Peak 0.9-meter telescope
image.credit: T. A. Rector (NRAO/AUI/NSF and NOIRLab/NSF/AURA) and M. Hanna (NOIRLab/NSF/AURA). Taken with the 0.9-meter telescope on Kitt Peak and the NOAO Mosaic camera. Resized to 600 × 612 and converted to AVIF; colors unchanged.

sections.title: The first galaxy seen to turn
sections.text: In 2005, radio astronomers tracked two water masers on opposite sides of the galaxy with the Very Long Baseline Array. For the first time, they could measure a galaxy’s rotation and its motion across the sky directly. It moves at about 190 km/s relative to the Milky Way, toward the Andromeda Galaxy, of which it may be a satellite.

sections.title: A nursery 1,500 light-years wide
sections.text: Northeast of the core lies NGC 604, one of the largest H II regions known, nearly 1,500 light-years across, with a spectrum similar to the Orion Nebula’s. William Herschel listed it separately from the galaxy, and it later received its own NGC number.

sections.title: Hubble’s other Cepheids
sections.text: In 1922–23, John Charles Duncan and Max Wolf found variable stars in the galaxy. In 1926, Edwin Hubble showed that 35 of them were Cepheids and estimated their distance, more evidence that spiral nebulae are galaxies of their own.

sections.title: A stream to Andromeda
sections.text: In 2004, astronomers announced a clumpy stream of hydrogen gas linking the Triangulum and Andromeda galaxies, a hint that the two have pulled on each other in the past. The discovery was confirmed in 2011.

sections.title: Measured to 1.3%
sections.text: Hubble Space Telescope photometry of 154 Cepheids, calibrated against the Large Magellanic Cloud, puts the galaxy 840,000 parsecs away, about 2.74 million light-years, with an uncertainty of just 1.3%.

source.title: Breuval et al. (2023): A 1.3% Distance to M33 from Hubble Space Telescope Cepheid Photometry
